name: No nuts no glory
text: [overview] From the southeast shore of Lake Agnes, head up steep, avalanche-prone snow on the climber's left side of the wall to an overhanging yellow cave.
[overview] P5 is 30 m of steep snow, about 60 degrees, angling left to a tree;
earlierWhy: why: Steep avalanche-prone snow leads to the wall, but nothing shows whether any glacier is involved. | secondReview: no/yes: Route above Lake Agnes on steep avalanche-prone snow and a wall, with no glacier in that basin.

name: Asteroid Alley
text: [approach] Walk up the glacier-tour road until it drops toward the ice, then follow an occasionally cairned trail up toward the prominent gully you can see from the lot, just below the icefall.
[approach] Stay low enough to keep off the glacier but high enough to avoid losing elevation.
earlierWhy: why: The approach stays off the glacier, but the descent and upper line were not confirmed as glacier-free.

name: Southwest Ridge
text: [beta] Above the tarns, cross a faint headwall right to left, follow the glacial stream to a shallow col, and cross the snowy plateau to the ridge.
[hazards] Snow slope needing axe and crampons.
[hazards] Glacier and snowfield travel.
[gear] Ice axe.
[gear] Crampons.
[turnaround] Turn back if the notches are wet or icy or the snow slope is too hard without crampons.
[pitch_detail] Snow.
[pitch_detail] Faint route across the headwall to a col and snowy plateau;
[pitch_detail] ice axe and crampons for the snow slope..
earlierWhy: why: Trip reports describe the so-called glacier as a permanent snow patch crossed with boots, axe or crampons. | secondReview: yes/yes: Reports describe a glacier and snowy plateau crossing on the normal line, soft or hard depending on the day.

name: Southern Comfort
earlierWhy: why: A winter ice and mixed line with no text, glacier absence not confirmed. | secondReview: no/yes: A winter line on Rundle limestone above Canmore, a mountain with no glacier, though the route itself was not found online.

name: North Face, East End
earlierWhy: why: Graded with steep snow and ice, no text, glacier absence not confirmed.

name: All That for a Hand Crack?
text: [approach] Parties camp on the level snow shelf beneath the west face, and the routes are spread along the foot of that face from camp.
[descent_text] After the second pitch, mantel above the anchor onto the snow, which leads to the descent line.
[descent_text] Walk off to the south over the snow, the same way as for the other routes on the west face.
earlierWhy: why: Camp is on a snow shelf and the descent is over snow; crevasses are named only for the other routes here.

name: Granitic Dreams
text: [overview] Length varies with snowpack: about 230 feet in June, with the first anchors near 140 feet, and at least 30-40 feet longer after summer melt.
[approach] Parties camp on the level snow shelf beneath the west face, and the routes are spread along the foot of that face from camp.
[descent_text] Walk off to the south over the snow, the same way as the other west face routes.
[descent_text] Rappelling this line is a poor idea because it is long, and snowmelt over the season lengthens it further.
earlierWhy: why: Same snow descent as the neighbouring routes, with no crevasse mention in its own text.

name: Mt. Michelson - North Ridge
text: [overview] this line climbs the ridge on the north side, lying between the two northern glaciers.
[overview] Esetuk Creek is followed beyond many forks over wet tundra, then rock, talus and boulder slopes holding snow into June;
[overview] Cross Esetuk Glacier close to the toe, climb steeper boulders to the ridge, then mostly snow steepening to about 45 degrees.
[overview] Early-season snow may be loose, with deep postholing.
[detailed_rack] Pickets are possible later in the season, once the snow is consolidated.
[approach] The ground is wet tundra giving way to talus and boulder slopes where snow lingers into June, and the travel is slow and tedious.
[approach] Go over the Esetuk Glacier close to its terminus to get to the root of the peak, then work up a steep boulder field to a higher point on the ridge, where the terrain turns to snow.
earlierWhy: why: It crosses the Esetuk Glacier near its toe; crevasse hazard there is not stated.

name: Didilkama Traverse
text: [overview] Beyond, descend toward the next tower and follow the ridge to the Snowbird Glacier, where route finding, rappels or hard downclimbing may be needed.
earlierWhy: why: It descends toward a glacier but crevasse hazard on the line is not stated.

name: North Couloir
earlierWhy: why: No page for this route was found; ice and couloir route with steep snow.

name: Goldfinger
text: [overview] good weather and dry conditions are hard to catch (snow near the summit, storms and water on pitch 3 turned parties back).
[overview] After lots of snowfall, start left of the main corner on easy ground to a ledge, after steep snow with a hidden moat (belay it).
earlierWhy: why: Snow near the summit and a hidden moat are mentioned only for wet seasons.

name: South Gully/Ridge
text: [overview] A wide snow couloir at 40-50 degrees, bending slightly right, runs for 1800 feet before it constricts, forks and kicks up.
[overview] The right fork rises several hundred feet more and may hold some combination of ice, snow and rock, possibly with moderate ice or mixed climbing.
[overview] a brief snow traverse at low angle leads to the next couloir, which turns left onto the south ridge.
[overview] The ridge is easy 4th class with gendarme bypasses to a snowfield summit.
[overview] The couloir funnels debris, so move quickly and early and watch snow conditions.
[detailed_rack] Natural gear, slung horns and perhaps a picket or two.
earlierWhy: why: A snow couloir 1,800 ft long; no glacier on the line is described.

name: Toe gully
text: [overview] Tools and crampons are optional.
[approach] Follow the first fault line up to the basin of the Cleveland Glacier, then continue up the basin to the obvious cliff band.
earlierWhy: why: It enters a glacier basin, but crampons and tools are called optional.

name: The Fall Line
earlierWhy: why: No text; it is on the Mendenhall Towers where the approach is glacial.

name: North Face
text: [overview] best in winter or spring, when the two main approaches are easier with snow cover.
[overview] The first goes up steep snow to a 30 ft rock band, then more snow with boulders suitable for sling anchors.
[overview] With the band snowed over it felt about 5.7 / M2+, and good gear turned up after digging.
[overview] The second is 55-degree snow up to the boulder on top (5.4, easier on the back side).
[detailed_rack] A picket or two is optional.
earlierWhy: why: A winter and spring ice route; a glacier is not mentioned.

name: Mt. Michelson, South Face
text: [overview] The southern side departs from the glacier of that name, covers 1000-2000' of loose blocks, talus and snow, and then follows a final line of snow and ice up to the crest of the summit ridge.
[detailed_rack] A few pickets and ice screws may help.
earlierWhy: why: Route leaves a glacier but the text does not say whether crevasses are met.

name: Col of the Wild
text: [overview] brief cruxes of ice or mixed rock appear now and then, with much simulclimbing on steep snow.
[overview] Near the top a large cornice may need tunneling.
[detailed_rack] Standard alpine rack: some small and medium cams, a nut selection, knifeblades, angles, screws for ice, specters and a few pickets.
earlierWhy: why: Long snow route; text silent on glacier travel.

name: Kissing up the choss pile
text: [approach] From the Reed Lakes lot, walk to the former building site, short of Nugget Boulder and the Snowbird slab.
[approach] Then take the path bearing left up the drainage, past the Snowbird mine on your right, and keep going up the bowls to the pass.
[approach] The Snowbird Glacier lies below the pass, and the Nunatak is the small formation beside it.
earlierWhy: why: Beside a small Alaska glacier below a pass; crevassing unknown. | secondReview: unsure/unsure: The formation sits beside the Snowbird Glacier below a pass, and sources do not say the line crosses it.

name: The Friends Along the Way
text: [overview] A couloir with over 2500 feet of gain, with snow close to vertical and traverses over chossy rock sections.
[overview] The first fork: steep snow if you go right, then 50 feet of steep choss;
[overview] going left means far steeper snow and some snow bridges.
[detailed_rack] A rope and a skeleton rack are worth carrying if snow anchors for descending are within your skills.
[what_to_bring] ice axe and crampons — required
earlierWhy: why: Steep couloir with snow bridges; glacier not stated.

name: Smoke em' if you got em'
text: [overview] Pitches 1-3 are the couloir (simul-climbing is possible depending on snow quality);
[detailed_rack] 3-6 snow pickets, cams from .5 to #2, and a full set of nuts.
earlierWhy: why: Snow couloir start; glacier not stated.
